content: Ancylostomiasis is a parasitic infection caused by hookworms, which are soil-transmitted helminths (STH). This condition is most commonly observed in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly in areas with low socioeconomic status. The infection is associated with a wide range of symptoms, including anorexia, flatulence, diarrhea, weight loss, pallor, shortness of breath, generalized weakness, edema, black tarry stools (melena), vomiting of blood (hematemesis), dizziness, fainting, coughing, sneezing, coughing up blood (hemoptysis), nausea, vomiting, throat irritation, and itchy, red, serpiginous skin lesions. The primary treatment for ancylostomiasis involves the use of anti-helminthic medications. The disease was first identified in 1838 by an Italian physician named Dubini. Hookworm infections can be classified into two main categories: human hookworms, which include Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus, and zoonotic hookworms, which include species such as Ancylostoma braziliense, Ancylostoma caninum, Ancylostoma ceylanicum, and Uncinaria stenocephala. The pathophysiology of ancylostomiasis involves the life cycle of the hookworm. Adult female hookworms residing in the small intestine of the host release eggs, which are excreted in the feces. Under favorable environmental conditions, these eggs hatch in the soil and develop into infective third-stage larvae (filariform larvae). These larvae can penetrate human skin or be ingested orally. Once inside the body, they enter the bloodstream, travel to the lungs, and migrate across the alveoli. From there, they ascend the bronchial tree to the pharynx, are swallowed, and eventually reach the small intestine, where they mature into adult worms capable of feeding on blood. The primary causative agents of ancylostomiasis are Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus. Less common causes include Ancylostoma braziliense, Ancylostoma caninum, Ancylostoma ceylanicum, and Uncinaria stenocephala. Ancylostomiasis must be differentiated from other conditions that present with similar symptoms, such as contact dermatitis, scabies, migratory myiasis, cercarial dermatitis, gastrointestinal bleeding due to portal hypertension, Meckel’s diverticulum, inflammatory bowel disease, NSAID-induced small bowel disease, angiectasias, adenocarcinoma, leiomyoma, and lymphoma. Globally, the prevalence of ancylostomiasis is estimated to affect approximately 1 billion people, with an incidence rate of 7.5 per 100 person-years. The condition is more common in men than women and disproportionately affects children and women of childbearing age. Mortality rates in tropical regions are estimated to be between 50,000 and 60,000 deaths annually. The majority of infected individuals remain asymptomatic, but symptoms can develop through direct skin contact with contaminated soil or via the fecal-oral route. Complications of the disease include iron deficiency anemia, impaired intellectual and cognitive development in children, and severe anemia, premature birth, and neonatal anemia in pregnant women. With appropriate treatment, the prognosis for ancylostomiasis is generally excellent. The diagnosis of ancylostomiasis is primarily made through microscopic examination of stool samples to detect hookworm eggs. Most patients are asymptomatic, but common symptoms include anorexia, flatulence, diarrhea, weight loss, pallor, shortness of breath, generalized weakness, edema, black tarry stools, vomiting of blood, dizziness, fainting, coughing, sneezing, coughing up blood, nausea, vomiting, throat irritation, and itchy, red, serpiginous skin lesions. Physical examination findings may include pallor, fatigue, dizziness, and the presence of serpiginous, erythematous, and palpable plaques associated with edema and abdominal distension. Laboratory findings often reveal decreased hemoglobin levels, eosinophilia, and the presence of live, motile worms during upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. Imaging studies, such as X-rays and CT scans, do not typically show findings specific to ancylostomiasis. Treatment involves the administration of anti-helminthic medications, with the efficacy of treatment varying based on the severity of the infection, geographic location, and patient age. In severe cases, blood transfusions and iron supplementation may be necessary. Surgical intervention is not recommended for managing this condition. Primary prevention strategies include periodic mass administration of anthelminthic medications to at-risk populations, avoiding barefoot contact with soil, and educating patients on proper hygiene and sanitation practices.
